about: Medemelacha (Medemblik), the king's toll on the inland water north of Dorestad. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/medemelacha.md and the spine; a draft for the user to overwrite. Nobody who lived here is named before 1118, so every resident is invented and says so; (?) marks what is not verified.

ports.summary: One row of some twenty thatched houses on the south bank of a peat stream, at the end of a sandy ridge in wide wet moss, a long day north of the Vecht mouth across the Almere. It is the king's ground: every hull that passes pays him a tenth, and a tenth of that tenth is Saint Martin's at Traiectum. A merchant comes to break the run between the Rhine and the terps, to sell Rhenish pots, querns, wine, iron and timber to people who have none, and to load cloth, hides, salt beef and cheese.
ports.seasons: The water opens at Easter and the Rhine boats come north with it; the cattle are driven in from the lake hamlets and killed and salted at Martinmas, when hides are cheap and salt is dear. In a hard frost the stream and the lake bear a man, and the boys go out on bone runners with pricker poles; at the thaw the bank is mended, each household its own length.

history.text: About this year the place begins, probably as a seasonal bank market for skippers between the Rhine and the terps; people soon stay the year round.
history.source: J. van Leeuwen, Middeleeuws Medemblik, West-Friese Archeologische Rapporten 61 (2014) 6.2; Archeologie in West-Friesland 13 (2014)

history.text: About this year, on Radbod's death, the country comes under the Franks. The place is the king's own, and he takes toll from every trader who sails past.
Pippin grants Saint Martin's at Traiectum a tenth of the king's income from his lands and tolls; the tenth here most likely goes back to this grant, which does not name the place (?).
history.source: WAR 61 2.2.2.1; the charter itself not seen (?)

history.text: About this year the law of the Frisians is written down: between the Vlie and the Sincfal a noble's life is 100 solidi, a free man's 50, a half-free man's 25, and Sunday work costs 4 solidi.
history.source: Lex Frisionum I and XVIII (tr. K. Nieuwenhuijsen, keesn.nl); the date is the usual one (?)

history.text: The first raids on this coast are written down: a Danish fleet of two hundred ships on the Frisian islands, and a hundred pounds of silver paid. What it did here is not recorded.
On the day after Christmas a storm flood goes over Frisia and 2,437 people are counted drowned. Its effect here is unknown.

Rorik the Dane is granted Dorestad 'and other counties'. That he held this toll is likely, not stated. About now 1,662 g of silver goes into the ground in a Badorf pot at Westerklief on Wieringen, nearly a day's walk north.
About this year Dorestad ends. The house row here lives on, perhaps because of its toll.
Godfrid the Dane is given Rorik's lands; he is killed in 885, and the Danish lords of western Frisia end with him.
On 4 August King Arnulf grants lands to Count Gerulf; the place probably stands under him and his heirs from now on.
About this year the place is first written down: 'In Medemolaca regalis decima', the king's tenth, in the goods register of Saint Martin's, drawn together about 918 under Bishop Balderik.

On 26 June King Otto, a child of five, gives Count Ansfried the king's share of toll, mint and rent at 'villa Medemelacha'. On 25 August at Nijmegen he gives Count Dirk his fief between the rivers Medemelacha and Chinnelosa as his own.
history.source: WAR 61 2.2.2.2 and 2.2.2.3; Wikipedia (nl) 'Dirk II van Holland'; the charters themselves not seen (?)

history.text: On 18 September Count Arnulf is killed at Winkel, half a day's walk west, fighting the West Frisians.
Ansfried becomes bishop of Traiectum, and Saint Martin's now holds all the king's income here.
King Henry gives Bishop William of Traiectum the count's rights in Westflinge, the first time the district is named.

eras.text: The king's toll in its quiet years. One row of houses ten paces back from a soft bank, Rhine boats nosed into the reeds, a king's man with a tally and a small wooden church of Saint Martin (?). The first two summers are hungry: the moss grows cattle, not bread.

The first fleets are on the islands. Nothing is written of a raid here, but silver goes under hearth stones and the cattle are kept further from the water. Trade goes on; the pots in the houses are still Badorf ware.
After the flood of Saint Stephen's day: the lake hamlets drowned, the cattle dead, salt in the wells, the bank torn out. Everything is wanted and there is no silver to pay with.

Danish lords over western Frisia. The toll is taken as before, by a Dane, for a Dane, in a Frankish king's name; silver is weighed as often as counted. Dorestad's boats come less each year, and after 863 not at all.

The counts' time. Dorestad is gone and the row has grown: more houses, thin turf walls, a byre at one end. The peat behind is being ditched and ploughed, and the boats from the south now come from Tiel and Daventre with Pingsdorf pots.

The bishop's toll. Count Ansfried has the king's share from 985 and takes it with him to Saint Martin's in 995. West of here the Frisians kill a count and owe nobody anything; a potter works on the row, combs are cut from antler, and the dead begin to be laid by the church.

sites.name: The south bank
sites.see: A peat-brown stream thirty paces wide and a low bank faced with stakes and wattle, a different man's work every few yards. Flat-bottomed Rhine boats lie nose-in among the reeds with planks run ashore; behind them the thatch of the row and grey sky to every edge. It smells of wet peat, tar and cattle.
sites.source: WAR 61 3.1.6, 6.2, 6.3: boats against the soft bank, each plot-holder his own revetment, the river about 30 m wide; no jetty has been found

sites.name: The king's ground
sites.see: An open piece of the bank where no house stands, with a row of oak posts driven in to mark the tenth part that is Saint Martin's. A bench, a balance hung from a pole, a heap of pots and a tethered cow taken in kind. The king's man sits with his back to the wind and counts hulls aloud.
sites.source: WAR 61 2.2.2.1 and 6.3: the toll and the tenth are sure; the open ground called Koningshof is a guess for where; the posts are as at Dorestad (?)

sites.name: The house row
sites.see: Long timber houses with daubed walls and reed thatch, ends to the water, a boat's length of working ground between each. Goods are sold from the plots: crates of Rhenish pots in straw, querns leaning on a wall, bolts of grey cloth over a rail, a cheese cut open to be tasted. Smoke comes out under the eaves and hangs.
sites.source: WAR 61 6.3: houses at least 10 by 5 m, some 10 m apart, plots square to the water; the wares are those of the finds (WAR 61 4.7, 4.8)

sites.name: Meinburg's house
sites.see: The third house from the stream mouth, the one with a boat's worth of strangers' shoes by the door. Inside a long hearth, benches, a vat of ale under a cloth and a green glass beaker nobody but the house's own may touch. The door post is cut with small marks, one house's sign under another, and a row of notches by each.
sites.source: invented; the house is as dug (WAR 61 6.3), the green funnel beaker is a find of the place (WAR 61 4.8), and skippers stopping over is the dossier's reading of why the place exists

sites.name: Saint Martin's
sites.see: A small church of upright oak planks on the highest bit of the ridge, thatched, with a wooden cross on the gable and no bell until someone gives one. Inside it is dim and smells of tallow; one candle of real wax stands by the altar for feast days. Beyond the door the moss runs flat to the edge of the world.
sites.source: WAR 61 2.3.2 and 6.3: a wooden church of Saint Martin is thought possible by 750-800 and likely by 850; none has been found (?). The name Boniface belongs to the later building

sites.name: The stone ground
sites.see: The working ground between two houses, grey with lava dust. Rough black quern stones off the Rhine boats are stacked like loaves; a man sits astride one with a pick, dressing the grinding face, and the chips fly into the nettles. One half-made stone has lain by the wall so long it has moss on it.
sites.source: WAR 61 6.3: a half-made lava quern, found 1982, suggests rough stones were finished here; the man is invented

sites.name: The barrel wells
sites.see: Behind each house a square frame of planks over a hooped stave barrel sunk in the sand, a bucket on a hide rope beside it. Women meet here at first light, and what the row knows it knows from the wells. The water is brown and sweet; after the great flood it is salt for a year.
sites.source: WAR 61 4.6.5.2: barrel wells at least 1.2 m high and 75 cm wide, one to a plot, 9th-10th century; the salt after 838 is the spine's (dorestad_falls)

sites.name: The lake hamlet
sites.see: A short walk south along the ridge, where it runs out into the reeds of the lake: one long house, ditches, two clay ovens in the open and rye on the dry strip. Cattle stand to the hock in wet grass. At Martinmas the beasts are driven from here to the bank, and the ground by the ovens is black with old fires.
sites.source: WAR 61 3.1.4 and 5.5: the hamlet at Schuitevoerderslaan, late 8th and early 9th century, a house of 6 by 20 m, perhaps two field ovens, given up before 900; cattle brought alive to be killed and salted for ships. The burnt patches were once read as salt-making, then doubted

sites.name: The eel stakes
sites.see: Where the stream runs out into the lake of Wervershoof: lines of stakes and wicker eel traps in the reeds, a punt pulled up, no house in sight and the king's ground hidden round the bend. By day herons. By night, now and then, two boats lying side by side without a light and the sound of something heavy being handed across.
sites.source: invented on the spine's hook (swords_north: 'where a cargo changes boats at night'); the lake and the stream mouth are WAR 61 1.1; eel fishing is likely, not dug (?)

sites.name: The trees on the ridge
sites.see: The only trees for a day's walk: alder, birch and a few old oaks on the sand, west of the last house. Under the biggest oak the grass is trodden, and there are things in the fork of it that nobody put there by accident: a cheese rind, a twist of wool, a cow's horn. Elk tracks cross the wet ground behind.
sites.source: Archeologie in West-Friesland 13: trees on the ridge, open moss beyond; WAR 61 2.3.2: the country round was still largely heathen in Carolingian times; elk bone of about 700 (WAR 61 4.10.2.8). The offering tree is invented (?)

people.name: Radward
people.trait: The king's toll-gatherer: slow, exact, and incurious about anything that is not afloat. He counts hulls the way other men say prayers.
people.want: A tally that comes out even when the king's man rides up from Dorestad, and Saint Martin's posts never moved by a hand's breadth.
people.fear: The king's envoys asking why two boats came down the Vecht and only one was counted here.
people.voice: Says the number first, then the thing. Never says 'about'.
people.looks: About forty-five, long and stooped, thin fair hair, a short grey Frisian cloak pinned at the shoulder, a bundle of notched hazel sticks at his belt and a balance in a wooden box.
knows: what the tenth comes to on any cargo, in kind or in pennies
which boats went north this moon and what they drew
the law between the Vlie and the Sincfal, by heart
that the count at Dorestad has no right here and would like one

ties.note: a tenth of what he takes is the bishop's, and he carries it to Traiectum himself each Martinmas
the toll is the king's, not the count's; the count sends men to ask what it yields
two men who cut tallies; they check each other's sticks and trust nobody else's
he knows what Eilbern does at the eel stakes and has never once caught him at it
her husband was his brother; he eats at her hearth and pays for it
the ferryman sends word ahead by the Vecht boats who is coming and how laden
the priest is the only other man on the row who reckons on a stick
the head of the old lords' terp says he counts Winaldum bolts longer than they are; he counts them as they lie (?)
the old prior counts the saint's tenth twice each Martinmas, and feeds him at the guest table while he does

lines.greet: One boat, four men, and she sits low. A tenth is the king's. Show me what is under the hides before you tell me what is there.
lines.greet_again: So it is you again, and that is good, because a man who comes twice was not drowned and was not hanged. What do you carry?
rumour: Three boats went north since the new moon and two came back. I do not say what happened to the third, I only say that I count.
The count's steward asked me what this toll yields, and I told him to ask the king, and he did not laugh.
They are writing our law down at the king's court, at fifty solidi for a free man. I was worth that before it was written.
lines.saying: The king takes a tenth and the saint a tenth of the tenth. Only the water takes all of it.
lines.trust: I am going to Traiectum at Martinmas with the saint's share. My boat leaks and yours does not, so think about it.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and go past me, not round me.

people.source: invented; the office is sure and the man unknown (WAR 61 2.2.2.1). The name is Rad- + -ward

people.name: Meinburg
people.trait: A widow who keeps the house where skippers sleep. She remembers every man who has eaten at her hearth, what he owed and what his boat was called.
people.want: Her house full at Easter and empty of fools by Pentecost; a husband for her daughter Radsuit who owns a boat and does not drown in it.
people.fear: A guest's theft or killing laid at her door, since the host answers for the stranger.
people.voice: Dry, quick, unsurprised. Asks after your crew by name before she asks after you.
people.looks: A little over forty, broad, red hands, a white linen head-cloth, a brown gown with two plain bronze brooches, a ring of keys and a small knife at her belt, a green glass beaker in her hand.
knows: who is in harbour, who has gone north and who is late
the price of salt beef, cheese and cloth along the row
which skipper will carry another man's goods, and which should not be asked
every mark on her door post and whose it is

ties.note: her dead husband's brother
two widows who lend on goods; Thiadburg's boats sleep here on the way north
he paid for her new roof and has never said what he wants for it
her sister's son; she feeds him and does not ask where he was last night
the weaver on the great terp, whose grey cloth she sells to the Rhine boats; they send each other word of bad payers
lets his buyers sleep on credit until the stones are paid
her granddaughter, Radsuit's girl, born about 800 and married out to the lake

lines.greet: A new boat is always welcome. Take your shoes off and hang your knife on the peg. Ale is a farthing's worth of anything you have, and the fire is free.
lines.greet_again: I know that step, so sit where you sat before. I cut your mark on the post the last time, which means that now you have to keep coming.
rumour: Thiadbod's big boat lay here two nights and unloaded nothing. A boat that unloads nothing has unloaded somewhere.
The priest wants a bell, and he has asked every skipper for one since Easter, so one of you will give in.
They say bread is four pennies the measure by the king's word. The king has not been to the terps.
lines.saying: A guest and a fish: both are best the first three days.
lines.trust: Your father's mark is on that post, and yours under it. Whatever you owe on the river, you owe nothing in this house.
lines.farewell: Come back dry. I do not rub marks out, but I have stopped cutting notches by a few.

people.source: invented; households of six to ten on the row and skippers breaking the run here (WAR 61 6.2, 6.3); the host's liability is the Kentish law of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15, used here by likeness (?). The name is Mein- + -burg

people.name: Eilbern
people.trait: A skipper with no goods of his own: he carries other men's for hire, by day for anyone and by night for those who pay double.
people.want: A boat that is his and not half his aunt's; enough silver to stop the night work before a king's man is waiting in the reeds.
people.fear: Being the one man named when a bigger man's cargo is found. He knows the law: all goods lost, and half to the finder.
people.voice: Easy, friendly, never finishes a sentence that could be repeated.
people.looks: Not yet thirty, lean, sunburnt, hair the colour of rope, a short patched cloak, bare feet, eel-skin thongs round his wrists and a punt pole never far from his hand.
knows: every channel of the Almere and the lake, in the dark
which boat from the south has something under its ballast
what a blade fetches at Sliesthorp, though he has never been there
where the king's man sits and when he sleeps

ties.note: shifts what Thiadbod will not be seen carrying past a toll
his mother's sister; half his boat is hers
a game the two of them have played for ten years
has never met him; the goods he hands on at night end at Asulf's booth, and so would the blame
the man at the Ems mouth who takes the load on from the last Frankish landing
the Westergo pilot talks all through a handing-over; Eilbern would rather it were done in the dark
confesses to him, briefly

lines.greet: You draw a hand less water than you should, for what you say you carry. I only mention it. I carry for hire, if you ever need a second bottom.
lines.greet_again: There he is! Are you still afloat, and still honest? One of those two wears off in the end.
rumour: A blade bought on the smiths' street sells for three in the north. I have that from a man who has that from a man.
The king's law says no mail coat leaves the realm. The law does not say which side of the eel stakes the realm stops.
Radward sleeps from the second cock to the first light, as everybody knows, which is exactly why I do not trust it.
lines.saying: The heron and I both fish at night, but only one of us pays a tenth.
lines.trust: If a fat man from Dorestat asks you to meet me at the stakes, ask him why he is not meeting me himself.
lines.farewell: A fair wind to you, and if anyone asks, I was asleep.

people.source: invented; skippers carrying other men's goods for hire are suggested for the place (WAR 61 6.3); the law is the capitulary of Thionville 805 c. 7 (spine, swords_north). The name is Eil- + -bern

people.name: Liudbrand
people.trait: The priest of a wooden church on the edge of the baptised world: schooled at Traiectum, sent north with one book and a great deal of patience.
people.want: A bell, wax, and wine enough for the Mass; one family from the lake hamlets at the font each Easter.
people.fear: Word from east of the Lauwers, where the churches burned; and that his people come to Mass for the market after it.
people.voice: Gentle and a little tired. Says a hard thing as if asking a favour.
people.looks: About thirty, thin, tonsured, a patched brown wool tunic to the ankle, a wooden cross, ink on two fingers and mud to the knee.
knows: the feasts and fasts and when the next one falls
what the bishop needs and will pay for: wax, wine, oil
who among the hamlet people still goes to the tree on the ridge, and why he says nothing
the letters, and a little of what is in his one book

ties.note: his bishop; Saint Martin's sent him and Saint Martin's has the tenth
heard him at Traiectum as a boy and still tells what he said about the terps
the toll man is the only other man here who reckons anything on a stick
hears his confession, which is short and leaves a great deal out
the priest at the martyr's church; they send each other wax and bad news
his old master at Saint Martin's, who sent him north with one book and still asks after it

lines.greet: God's welcome to you. You have come a long way to a small church, and if you have wax aboard, I will not pretend that I am not interested.
lines.greet_again: You came back. I said a prayer for your boat; I am glad to see what it was worth.
rumour: East of the Lauwers they burned the churches this year. The priests will go back, as the priests always do.
The bishop writes that grain must be sold at the king's price. He does not write where I am to find the grain.
A man at the lake still leaves cheese in a tree, though I baptised him at Easter, and I think he is only being careful.
lines.saying: Saint Martin cut his cloak in half for a beggar. Here they would say he sold a short cloak at the long price.
lines.trust: I cannot pay you. But I write to Traiectum each Martinmas, and I can write your name where the bishop reads it.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and keep the fast aboard if your men will bear it, and do not fight them if they will not.

people.source: invented; a priest here is 'perhaps' (WAR 61 2.3.2), the church a possible base for the mission to the terps (WAR 61 6.3). The churches burned east of the Lauwers in 793 (spine, cross_and_grove). The cloak joke turns Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34. The name is Liud- + -brand

people.name: Tado
people.trait: Dresses rough black quern stones from the Rhine into stones a woman can turn. Half deaf from the pick; judges every stone, and every man, by the sound it makes when struck.
people.want: Sound roughouts from Colonia, not the cracked ones the dealers keep for Frisians; a buyer across the sea, now that the English shore is shut.
people.fear: A flaw he did not hear, found by a buyer; his hands going before his son can dress a face true.
people.voice: Loud, because he cannot hear himself. Knocks on things while he talks.
people.looks: Near forty, short, thick in the shoulder, grey lava dust in his hair and beard, a leather apron, a short iron pick, a rag tied over one eye that a chip took.
knows: a sound stone from a flawed one, by ear
what a pair of querns costs at Colonia, here, and on a terp
that the English king asked for black stones of a certain length, and nobody here knows what length
which Rhine skipper brings good stone

ties.note: takes his roughouts on credit each spring and pays in dressed pairs
Thiadbod buys finished stones at Dorestad and undersells him on the terps
she lets his buyers sleep on credit until the stones are paid
has never seen him; the reeve who turns Frankish hulls away has cost him two summers' stones

lines.greet: Go on and knock on it, and hear how it rings! That is a stone that will grind for your grandchildren, and the one beside it will split by Christmas.
lines.greet_again: Here is the man who listens, where most of them only look. What do you need, a pair or a boatload?
rumour: The English will not let a Frankish hull land, so my stones sit where they are. Stone keeps well enough, but I do not keep as well as stone.
Somebody at the king's court is arguing with the English king about the length of stones. Ask him what length he wants, and I will cut it.
The dealer at Colonia sends his cracked ones north, because he thinks that a Frisian cannot hear, and he is half right about that.
lines.saying: A quern and a wife: you learn in the first week whether she is sound, and by then you have paid.
lines.trust: You mean that one by the wall with the moss on it. I started it the year my father died, and it is not for sale, though you may ask me again next year.
lines.farewell: Mind your keel. A pair of my stones in the wrong place will take you down by the head.

people.source: invented; 'perhaps a finisher of rough quern stones' (WAR 61 6.3, the half-made quern found 1982). The black stones and their length are Charlemagne's letter to Offa, 796 (spine, black_stones). The name is a short form of a Thiad- name

people.name: Adelgard
people.trait: Mistress of the long house at the lake: cattle, cheese, rye on the dry strip. After the flood she is the one who counts who is left and what each needs.
people.want: Breeding stock, seed rye and timber after the water; before it, a fair price at Martinmas and a daughter married onto dry ground.
people.fear: The north-west wind at a spring tide. She will not say the word flood on the feast of Stephen.
people.voice: Blunt, unhurried. Reckons in cows, and tells you what a thing is worth in them.
people.looks: In the flood year near forty, tall, weathered, a grey wool gown kilted up for mud, bare forearms, a head-cloth tied behind, a cheese knife and a cow's lead rope over her shoulder.
knows: what every household on the lake lost, by name and by head of cattle
who can pay now, who can pay in three years and who never will
the price of a salted beast, a cheese and a bolt of grey cloth
which wells are sweet again

ties.note: Meinburg's granddaughter, Radsuit's girl, married out to the lake
pays his tenth in cheese and counts every one aloud in front of him
like every household here in his time she owes the lord's tenth, whoever the lord is

the canon Odulf spoke for the hamlet when Saint Martin's cellarer forgave its tenth the year after the water, and she has not forgotten (old Hadda of the 790s was long dead; the cellarer of 839 is not named)

lines.greet: You are from the south. Then you have grain, or timber, or you have wasted the trip.
lines.greet_again: You are the one who came back, and I am glad of it. My cows know your boat now, and they think it means salt.
rumour: They counted the drowned along the coast, and it came to two thousand four hundred and some. I did not need a clerk to count ours, which were eleven.
The wells are salt, so the cows will not drink and the ale tastes of the sea. Bring casks with you, even empty ones.
They say that Dorestat has burned again, as they say every year now, and one year it will not be worth saying.
lines.saying: Cattle die and kinsmen die, and the Danes have a verse about it, where we have the water.
lines.trust: I have no silver, but I have a tally stick and my word, and three heifers in calf by spring. Take the stick, and you will not be sorry that you did.
lines.farewell: Go on, then, and watch the sky to the north-west, as I do.

people.source: invented; farmers of the lake hamlets brought cattle to be killed and salted (WAR 61 5.5); the flood and its count are the Annals of St Bertin; its effect here is unknown and is the game's. Her saying leans on Hávamál 76-77 (texts_793.json). The name is Adel- + -gard

people.name: Gunnulf
people.trait: A Dane of Rorik's following set to take a Frankish king's tenth on a Frisian stream. He weighs where the last man counted, and trusts cut silver over any king's face.
people.want: The tenth full, a wife from the row, and his own share safe in the ground on Wieringen where no lord will ask after it.
people.fear: That Rorik sails for a kingdom in Denmark and leaves him here among people who remember everything.
people.voice: Slow Frisian with the words in a Danish order. Laughs before the joke, not after.
people.looks: About thirty-five, big, fair, a plaited beard, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic, a silver arm ring with hack marks in it, a folding balance in a bronze case and a small hammer on a thong under his shirt.
knows: the weight of silver in ounces and in the northern ortugs
which fleets are Rorik's and which are nobody's
what is wanted at Sliesthorp this summer
where on Wieringen a careful man puts a pot in the ground, though he will not say so sober

ties.note: his lord, as far as the sources let anyone say Rorik held this toll (?)
the toll man at Dorestad; they came over in the same ship and compare weights
she pays in cheese and he has never won an argument with her
left Denmark because the king's men wanted him; he does not say why
the terp lord who thinks someone on the Almere shore tells the Danes which mounds have had a good year (?)

lines.greet: It is a tenth, and you may call it the king's, the count's or my lord's as you like, because it weighs the same. Put it on the pan.
lines.greet_again: Here is the Frisian who does not argue, so sit down. I will weigh quickly, and then we will drink slowly.
rumour: There is a fleet on the islands that is not my lord's. I say this so you do not blame me later.
I take your Frankish pennies by weight, because a king can make a coin lighter, but he cannot make my balance lie.
Rorik goes to the king at Nijmegen. Kings want to see him often, because they do not sleep well when they cannot.
lines.saying: A Frisian counts his silver and a Dane weighs it, and a wise man does both and buries half.
lines.trust: If I am not here next summer, go to the west cliff on Wieringen and look where the gorse is oldest. I will say no more.
lines.farewell: Sail well, and if you meet ships with their shields out, tell them whose water this is, which may help.

people.source: invented; Danish lords over western Frisia 841-885 and Rorik's likely hold on the place (WAR 61 2.3.3); the Westerklief hoards of about 850 and about 880 (WAR 61 5.2.1; hoards_793.json westerklief). No Dane is recorded as living here. The name is Gunn- + -ulfr (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Ansfried
people.trait: Count of Huy, a soldier of the Ottos grown old and devout, who holds the king's share of this toll from 985 and becomes bishop of Traiectum in 995 against his will (?).
people.want: The toll honestly taken and given to God's use; quiet; to be let alone to pray.
people.fear: Blood on his hands again. As bishop he will not carry a sword. From about 1005 he fears nothing he can see: he is blind.
people.voice: Low, courteous, a man who has given orders all his life and is trying to stop.
people.looks: In 985 past forty, tall, spare, grey hair cut short, a plain dark cloak with a gold pin, a sword he wears from habit; after 995 a bishop's ring and staff and no sword; after 1005 led by a clerk's hand.
knows: what the king's charter of 985 gives him here: toll, mint and rent
the court of the Ottos, and who is rising in it
that Count Dirk has his own charter for the land between the two streams
the roads and tolls from the Maas to the Vlie

ties.note: not the man but his house: Saint Martin's, whose goods register first wrote this place down, and whose bishop he becomes
Count Dirk II, given his fief here as his own at Nijmegen two months after Ansfried's charter
never met; in his last years the fleets are back on the rivers, and Tiel and Traiectum burn the year before he dies (?)
a merchant of the Stathe who trusts a blind bishop's word over a count's seal

lines.greet: You are the shipman they told me of. I hold the king's share here. Tell me plainly what the toll man takes, and whether it is what he writes.
lines.greet_again: Come and sit down. I know your voice, which is most of what I know of anyone now.
rumour: The king is five years old and has given me a toll. When he is grown he may want it back, as kings do.
West of here they pay the count nothing, and say so. One day a count will go and ask them for it, though I would not be the one.
I am told I am to be a bishop. I have told them I am a soldier. They say the two have been known to meet.
lines.saying: I carried a sword for three kings, and the toll is harder, because a sword only wants one thing from you.
lines.trust: Bring me what Saint Martin's needs and I will set my seal to your freedom of this toll. I can still find the wax with my thumb.
lines.farewell: God keep you on the water. I will remember you in the morning office, if they tell me it is morning.

people.source: Otto III's charter of 26 June 985 (WAR 61 2.2.2.2); bishop 995-1010, blind from about 1005, died 3 May 1010 (Wikipedia (nl) 'Ansfried'). That he ever came here himself is not recorded (?); his unwillingness to be bishop and his sword are Thietmar of Merseburg IV, from memory (?). The character is invented

stories.title: The boats at the eel stakes
stories.summary: North of Dorestad the count's eye does not reach, and the king's toll man sleeps. A cargo that left Colonia as wine comes out of the lake of Wervershoof in another man's boat, and somebody has to be that other man.
stories.picture: Two low boats side by side in black reeds under a thin moon, no lamp; a man handing a long bundle wrapped in hide across the gap, another looking back toward a single far light on the bank.

beats.text: Thiadbod, friendly as ever, asks whether you are going north by the Almere, and whether you would lie a night at the eel stakes below Medemelacha for a man called Eilbern. He does not say why. He names a price that says why.

At the stakes Eilbern brings his boat alongside without a light. Twelve bundles, each as long as an arm and heavier than it looks, to go on to the Ems mouth. You may take them, refuse them, or ask to see inside one.
In the morning the toll man counts your hull and looks at your waterline for a long breath. He says a boat that came in light and goes out deep has found something in a place with nothing to sell.

At the last Frankish landing before the Danes a skipper takes the bundles and pays in weighed silver. He lets fall the name of the man they are for: Asulf, at Sliesthorp, who pays for blades in people.
Meinburg sets your ale down hard. She has heard. She says her sister's son will hang for a fat man's silver one day, and asks whether you mean to be standing beside him.

endings.how: Took the bundles north and handed them on (sets sw_ran_blades; at Emuthon sw_buyer_known).
endings.text: The silver is the best you have had for a week's work, and Eilbern calls you partner. Radward counts your hull twice from then on, and says nothing, which from him is a great deal.
endings.reward: 240 d in weighed silver; Eilbern a fast friend who will carry for you at night on the Almere; the buyer's name in the north; Radward cool.

endings.how: Went to Radward and said what lies at the stakes, naming no one but Thiadbod.
endings.text: Radward goes out with two men before light and finds the bundles and no skipper. Half the goods are the finder's by the king's law. He cuts you a stick that says your hull passes here untolled, and Eilbern does not speak to you for a year.
endings.reward: A charter of toll freedom at Medemelacha (unlock_charter_medemelacha); a half share of the seized goods, about 180 d; Thiadbod your open enemy; Eilbern wary.

endings.how: Refused the load, and lent Eilbern the price of the other half of his boat so that he need not take the next one.
endings.text: Eilbern buys his aunt's half and carries cheese and querns by daylight, complaining. Meinburg cuts a second notch by your mark for no call at all. Thiadbod finds another man, further north.
endings.reward: Eilbern as a sworn partner with a second bottom on the inland water (unlock_partner_eilbern); Meinburg a fast friend; the loan back in three years, in freight carried free.

stories.reward: By the ending: weighed silver and a night carrier, or the toll's freedom, or a partner with a boat.

stories.title: Bread for cloaks
stories.summary: The harvest of 792 failed and the moss grows cattle, not corn: the row and the lake hamlets buy their bread every year, and this year there is none to buy. They will pay in cloth, cheese, hides, or a daughter's dowry silver.
stories.picture: A boat at the soft bank with open grain sacks; a line of women with folded grey cloaks and cheeses in their arms; a priest standing between with a wooden measure, the toll man watching from his bench.

beats.text: At the wells they are not talking about prices. A woman asks straight out whether you have rye aboard, and three others stop drawing water to hear the answer.
No one on the row has coin for grain. They offer a cloak for a sack, then two; a cheese; a bundle of hides; and one man, not meeting your eye, a string of silver that was to go with his daughter.

Liudbrand has the bishop's word that grain is to be sold by the king's measure and at the king's price. He asks you, as a favour, to let him hold the measure. He will write to Traiectum who sold fair.
At Saint Martin's the cellarer knows your name from a letter out of the north. The bishop has wax to buy and wine to move, and would rather give the freight to a man the poor have prayed for.
On the great terp it is the same and worse: a lord's household that will pay in gold for what the row paid for in cloaks. What you sold at Medemelacha is already known here.

endings.how: Sold by the priest's measure at or under the king's price, and took cloaks and cheese for what silver could not cover (sets hy_fed_poor).
endings.text: You leave with a hold of grey cloth worth more in Colonia than the grain was worth here, and a letter gone south ahead of you. For years afterwards there is a cheese on your thwart when you wake at this bank.
endings.reward: Frisian cloth and cheese worth about 150 d over the grain's cost; the church's standing here and at Traiectum; a standing freight of wax and wine for Saint Martin's; Meinburg and Liudbrand friendly.

endings.how: Took the dowry silver and the double cloaks (sets hy_sold_dear).
endings.text: It is the best sale of the year. Radward takes his tenth of it without a word and the priest writes a different letter. The man's daughter is married two years late, to a worse match, and the row knows why.
endings.reward: About 320 d clear; the row cool for a generation; the count's men may ask about it at Dorestad.

endings.how: Landed part of the grain for nothing, at the church door.
endings.text: Nobody thanks you much; Frisians do not. But your mark goes on Meinburg's post with a cross cut over it, and when your own house is short one winter a boat comes down the Vecht with salt beef and no bill.
endings.reward: A deed the church remembers along the whole coast; every person here friendly; in a later lean year, provisions for a voyage sent free.

stories.reward: Cloth at a hungry price, the bishop's freight, and a place where the house is owed something better than silver.

stories.title: The share of the hundred pounds
stories.summary: In the summer of 810 two hundred Danish ships lie on the islands, three fights are lost, and the Frisians are to pay a hundred pounds of silver. Each place is told its share. The row has pots, cloth and cattle, and almost no coin.
stories.picture: The king's ground at dusk: a balance hung from a pole, the whole row standing round it with rings, brooches, hack silver and a few pennies in their hands; far off on the water, a line of dark hulls.

beats.text: You brought the word before the ships came. The cattle are already inland and the church's one cup is under a hearth stone. Radward says, for once without counting, that the row will not forget who rowed through the night.
The share is told: so many pounds from the row and the lake. Radward weighs what there is: brooches, a dowry string, the toll's own pennies. It is short by the weight of a man's two hands of silver.

Meinburg puts the green glass beaker on the table. It came from the Rhine before she was born. She asks what it would fetch at Dorestad, and whether you could be there and back before the Danes lose patience.
At the Ems mouth it is the same reckoning on every terp, and Aldger's own people are weighing out their share. A man who has paid his is given a cut stick to show the fleet.
The king of the Danes is dead before the year is out, killed by his own man, and the fleet went home. The row still has its houses. They say the silver bought that, and they say it to you by name.

endings.how: Put your own silver on the pan to make up the row's share (sets gf_paid_share).
endings.text: The Danes take the weight and leave the stream alone. Radward cuts a tally for what the row owes you and every household puts its mark on it. It is paid over six years, in cloth and salt beef, to the last ounce.
endings.reward: The loan back at half as much again, in goods at their price here; the fleet lets your hull be that season; a house plot on the row given by the neighbours (unlock_plot_medemelacha).

endings.how: Carried the row's glass, brooches and cloth to Dorestad, sold them well, and came back with coin in time.
endings.text: You were four days. The share is paid in pennies that were Meinburg's beaker a week ago. She says a house can drink out of wood. Years later you may find her a green glass one on the Rhine, or not.
endings.reward: A tenth of the sale as your fee, about 60 d; Meinburg a fast friend; a small errand left open for the house: a green glass beaker from Colonia.

endings.how: Had no silver to spare, or did not spare it, and left before the weighing was done.
endings.text: The row pays short and the Danes take cattle for the rest, and two boys with them. Nobody blames a stranger for being a stranger. Your mark stays on the post. The notches beside it stop for a while.
endings.reward: Nothing lost; the row cool until a service mends it; cattle and hides dear here for two years.

stories.reward: A plot on the row and a debt the whole place owes the house, or a friend for life in the house where the skippers sleep.

stories.title: Salt in the wells
stories.summary: The winter after the flood of Saint Stephen's day 838. The lake hamlets are drowned, the cattle dead, the wells salt and the bank gone; everything is wanted and there is nothing to pay with but a tally stick and a woman's word.
stories.picture: Grey winter light on flat water where fields were; one long house standing to its eaves in it, dead cattle on a ridge of sand, a tall woman in a kilted gown counting on her fingers beside a beached boat.

beats.text: The bank you knew is torn out for half its length and there is a boat lying in the nettles behind the row. The houses stand. The first thing anyone asks you for is not bread but a cask that will hold sweet water.

Adelgard has counted: eleven drowned on the lake, nine beasts in ten gone, the seed rye spoiled. She needs grain till harvest, timber for the bank, and heifers by spring. She has no silver. She holds out a notched stick.

Saint Martin's cellarer will forgive the hamlets their tenth for a year, if someone who has seen it will swear before him to what the water did. He also has oak he would sell to a man who can carry it.
On the IJssel there is timber and seed corn at a plain price, and nobody there has heard yet how bad it is in the north. What you say here will set the price for the boats behind you.
There are calves on the dry strip again. Adelgard brings out the stick, lays it beside yours, and they fit. She begins to pay.

endings.how: Sold grain, timber and stock on the tally, for nothing in the hand.
endings.text: For three years the house carries a debt nobody at Dorestad would lend against. Then the lake pays: cheese, cloth, salt beef, every Martinmas, a third over what was owed, and after Adelgard her daughter, and after you your heir.
endings.reward: The cargo's worth back twofold over six years, in goods; a standing first choice of the Martinmas beef and cheese at the hamlet's own price; a factor on the row who keeps your goods (unlock_factor_medemelacha); Adelgard a fast friend, and her heirs after her.

endings.how: Went to Traiectum, swore to what the water did, and brought back the bishop's oak and his word that the tenth is forgiven.
endings.text: The cellarer writes it down. The bank is mended with church oak, each household its own length, and one length more that they give to you. A year on, your name is read in Saint Martin's among those who did the church a service.
endings.reward: A length of revetted bank of your own on the row (unlock_plot_medemelacha); the church's standing at Traiectum; freight paid by Saint Martin's, about 120 d.

endings.how: Sold only for what silver the row could find, at the price of a wanting place.
endings.text: It is not much silver, and it is all they had. You are within your rights and everyone says so. The next spring a Daventre boat is selling on the tally, and it is her mark that goes on Adelgard's door.
endings.reward: About 200 d at once; no debt carried; the lake buys from another house from then on.

stories.reward: A debt that pays for a generation and a place where the house's stick is good, or a length of the bank, or quick silver and no welcome.

stories.title: The marks on the door post
stories.summary: Meinburg cuts the sign of every skipper who sleeps under her roof into her door post, and a notch for each time he comes back. The post outlives her; her daughter keeps it, and her daughter's daughter. A house with enough notches on it is not a stranger's house.
stories.picture: A dark oak door post close up, cut with rows of small signs and notches worn smooth by hands; a woman's hand with a small knife adding one; firelight behind, a pair of wet sea shoes on the threshold.

beats.text: The first night Meinburg asks what your boat's mark is, and cuts it into the post below a dozen others. She says it is so she knows whose shoes to throw out. Some of the marks have a long row of notches. Some have one, and a line cut through.
Four notches. Your place on the bench is kept without your asking, and she tells you what she would not tell a new boat: who is buying, who is lying, and what Thiadbod's man unloaded in the dark.

Eight. Radward nods to you before he counts your hull. Tado knocks on a pair of stones he has been keeping back. Meinburg asks, as if it were nothing, whether your boat could use a second man, and whether you have met her daughter.
The woman at the hearth is not Meinburg. She looks at you, then at the post, then puts her finger on a mark low down and worn pale. 'That one. You have his walk. Sit where he sat.'
At Dorestad a skipper you do not know asks whether you are the house with eight notches at Meinburg's. He has a cargo for the north and wants a name the row will take on trust.

endings.how: Kept coming back until the row counted you its own, and took the plot that was offered.
endings.text: The house has a length of bank, a barrel well and a mark on a post that three generations of one family have cut notches by. When Dorestad is gone, this is where the house is from.
endings.reward: A plot and the row's trust (unlock_plot_medemelacha); credit at every house here without a pledge; the heir starts with every feeling here whole instead of halved.

endings.how: Married into Meinburg's house, or fostered a child there.
endings.text: Radsuit, or her daughter, keeps the hearth and the post; your boats sleep free and your news is never a week old. The line cut through a mark is explained to you at last: a man who did not pay, and a man who drowned. She will not say which was which.
endings.reward: Kin on the inland water (unlock_kin_meinburgs_house); free lodging and provisions here; rumours here always fresh.

endings.how: Left a debt unpaid on the row, or a guest's harm at her door.
endings.text: She does not shout. She takes the small knife and cuts one line through your mark, and the notches stop. It can be mended, by the debt paid double before witnesses at the king's ground, once.
endings.reward: Nothing; lodging refused and every feeling here cool until it is mended.

stories.reward: A home port that is not Dorestad, and people in it who know the house by its mark across three lifetimes.

stories.title: The saint's share
stories.summary: A tenth of the king's tenth at Medemelacha is Saint Martin's, and the toll man carries it to Traiectum himself each Martinmas in a boat that leaks. The year he trusts it to another hull, that hull's master finds out what a toll man's trust is worth.
stories.picture: A long stooped toll man on a river bank holding out a sealed leather bag in both hands toward a small boat, a stack of cheeses and folded hides at his feet, his own boat lying hauled out and plainly leaking behind him.

beats.text: Radward stands over a sealed bag, eleven cheeses, four hides and a pot of butter, and looks at his own boat. He has never let the saint's share out of his hands. He asks you to keep it dry as far as Traiectum.
The keeper of the prior's store counts it once for the saint and once for the toll man, finds the seal whole, and cuts a stick: received, and by whose hull.
Radward reads the prior's stick with his thumb, then cuts one of his own. Your hull passes the king's ground untolled for as long as he sits on that bench.
Meinburg has heard. She says her husband's brother has cut six such sticks in twenty years, and that none of the six men was ever a fool.

endings.how: You carried the saint's share to Traiectum and brought back the prior's stick.
endings.text: The toll man cuts you a stick of his own. He still counts your hull aloud as you pass; he cannot help it. He does not ask what is under the hides.
endings.reward: flag unlock_charter_medemelacha: no toll at Medemelacha; the deed kept_commission; a word for the house in the toll man's Martinmas reckoning at Saint Martin's.

endings.how: You brought it a cheese short, and blamed the Almere.
endings.text: The prior writes down ten. Radward reads it and says the Almere does not eat cheese. He takes the saint's share south himself next year, in the boat that leaks, and bails.
endings.reward: One cheese; the toll man cool for as long as he remembers, which is until he dies.

endings.how: You said your boat was bound the other way.
endings.text: Radward nods and loads his own boat. He is three days late at the guest table and wet to the hip. Nothing is said, then or afterwards.

stories.reward: Freedom of the king's toll at Medemelacha, from the one toll man on the coast who cannot be given anything.

works.name: A length of the bank
works.what: A plot on the row, square to the water, with its own revetment of oak stakes and wattle to keep up: the way every householder here holds his ground.
works.needs: The row's good will: four calls at Meinburg's house, or a service to the place in a bad year.
works.gives: A place of your own to lie and to store goods; the toll man counts you as of the place; the first step to everything else here.
works.picture: A fresh line of pale oak stakes and woven wattle along a muddy bank, a small boat nosed against it, two men ramming a stake with a wooden beetle.
works.source: WAR 61 3.1.6, 6.2, 6.3: plots square to the water, each plot-holder his own revetment; revetments of about 800-1350 dug to January 2026 (archeologiewestfriesland.nl)

works.name: A jetty of your own
works.what: A short staging of oak piles and planks run out from your bank over the soft edge, so that a loaded boat can lie afloat at any water and be worked without wading.
works.needs: A length of the bank; oak, which must be brought: the ridge has few trees fit for piles.
works.gives: Loading and unloading in half the time; a heavier ship can lie here; other skippers pay you a little to use it.
works.picture: A narrow plank staging on rough piles reaching out through reeds into brown water, a boat alongside, a man rolling a cask down it.
works.source: The ports table gives the landing as a jetty; no jetty has been found and how the harbour looked is unknown (Archeologie in West-Friesland 13). Staging of this kind is known at Dorestad (?)

works.name: A salting house
works.what: A shed with a clay floor, troughs and hooks at the end of your plot, where the lake people's cattle are killed at Martinmas and laid down in salt for ships.
works.needs: A length of the bank; salt in the hold at Martinmas; the lake hamlet's friendship.
works.gives: Salt beef and hides at their source each Martinmas at the low price; ship's provisions here for nothing; a share for the hamlet that keeps them selling to you first.
works.picture: A low thatched shed open at one end, sides of beef on hooks, a wooden trough white with salt, cattle waiting in a pen, breath smoking in cold air.
works.source: WAR 61 5.5: live cattle brought in from the lake hamlets to be slaughtered and salted for ships; the building is invented

works.name: A bell for Saint Martin's
works.what: A hand bell of riveted iron sheet dipped in bronze, of the kind the missions carry, hung in a frame by the church door to call the row to Mass and to be rung in fog.
works.needs: Bought at Colonia or Traiectum and carried here whole; the priest's asking.
works.gives: The church's standing here and at Traiectum; the priest writes your name to the bishop; in fog the bell is rung for boats on the lake, and yours is seldom lost off this bank.
works.picture: A small dark four-sided bell with a loop handle hanging in a wooden frame beside a plank church door, a thin priest reaching up to it, mist behind.
works.source: Riveted iron hand bells are the mission's own kind of bell in these centuries (the Irish and Rhineland examples) (?); no bell is recorded here; the church itself is probable, not found (WAR 61 6.3)

works.name: A sweet well after the flood
works.what: A new barrel well sunk on the highest sand of the ridge, above where the salt water stood, with a plank frame and a lid, for the whole row to draw from.
works.needs: The flood of Saint Stephen's day 838; two sound wine casks with their hoops, knocked through.
works.gives: The row has water that cattle and brewers can use a year before the old wells clear; every person here a step warmer toward the house; water for your own casks for good.
works.picture: Three men lowering a hooped cask into a square pit in pale sand, a woman with a yoke and two buckets waiting, grey flood water lying in the low ground beyond.
works.source: WAR 61 4.6.5.2: barrel wells, a square timber frame over a hooped stave barrel; the salt wells after 838 are the spine's (dorestad_falls) and the game's

ships.note: The boat of the lake and the eel stakes: every household has one, and one is always for sale after a death or a bad winter.
ships.picture: A small tarred plank boat pulled up in reeds beside wicker eel traps, a pole and a single oar laid in it.
ships.source: invented on the setting (WAR 61 1.1: stream, lake and Almere); no boat has been dug here

ships.note: The inland freighter of the Rhine and the Vecht, the kind that brings the pots and querns north; an old one can be had from a skipper who is giving up the run.
ships.picture: A long, low, round-bottomed boat with a raised plank side, nosed into a soft bank, crates of pots in straw amidships.
ships.source: ships.md (the forerunner of the Utrecht type); the route Kromme Rijn, Vecht, Almere is WAR 61 1.1

ships.note: A flat-bottomed barge with its skipper, hired by the trip for querns, timber or cattle across the fresh water of the Almere; no good beyond the Vlie.
ships.picture: A flat plank barge deep with black quern stones, one man poling at the stern across wide still water.
ships.source: WAR 61 6.3: skippers who perhaps carried other men's goods for hire; the barge is ships.md

ships.note: A beach-landing coaster of the terp run, sold here now and then where the inland water meets the Vlie. Nothing is built to order: there is no yard, and the oak must come from the Rhine.
ships.picture: A broad clinker boat of ten paces with one mast and a furled sail, lying aground on a mud edge at low water, a man tarring her side.
ships.source: invented; no shipyard is evidenced here (the dossier, section 8)

sayings.text: The king takes a tenth and the saint a tenth of the tenth. Only the water takes all of it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the regalis decima of Saint Martin's (WAR 61 2.2.2.1)

sayings.text: A wound is paid by the inch here. So keep your knife short and your temper shorter.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Lex Frisionum, Additio III: among the western Frisians a wound is paid for by its length

sayings.text: Work on a Sunday costs four solidi. Rest on a Monday costs more, but nobody has written that one down.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Lex Frisionum XVIII

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self.
sayings.source: Hávamál 76-77 (Bellows 1923), as in texts_793.json; said here after the murrain of 810 and the flood of 838, by people who have it from the Danes

sayings.text: The king wanted to know what use our cloaks were, since he could not cover himself in bed with one. We told him: we are not in bed. We are at work.
sayings.source: a Frisian's answer, invented, to Charlemagne's complaint about the short cloaks sold at the long price (Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34, tr. Grant 1907, retold not quoted)

sayings.text: Riddle of the row: I am black, I came down a river whole and was given a mouth here; I eat every day and am never fed. (A quern.)
sayings.source: invented in the manner of the Exeter riddles; the lava querns finished here (WAR 61 6.3)

sayings.text: This year the water came over the land on the day after the Lord's birth, and more men were counted dead than any man here had ever seen living.
sayings.source: invented in the Chronicle's voice, on the Annals of St Bertin for 838-839: 2,437 drowned

sayings.text: Mighty in cows, the bishop. Well, somebody has to be.
sayings.source: a turn on Alcuin's greeting to a bishop of Traiectum as 'vaccipotens' (Design/content/peoples/frisian.md; the letter itself not seen (?))

easter_eggs.text: Ask anyone on the row whether great King Radbod kept his hall here and they will look at you kindly. Nobody has heard of it. In seven hundred years a chronicler will be sure of it, and a castle will carry his name.
easter_eggs.source: The Radbod story is of 1517 and 1767; the castle is of the 1280s; nothing shows Radbod was ever here (WAR 61 2.1.1, 2.3.1; Wikipedia (nl) 'Kasteel Radboud')

easter_eggs.text: An elk's toe bone, yellow with age, hangs on a thong by Meinburg's hearth. Her grandfather killed the beast on the wet ground behind the ridge. There are still elk; you may see the tracks.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 4.10.2.8: an elk's toe bone of about 700, and others

easter_eggs.text: After about 960 a comb-maker on the row sells an antler comb with a line of neat signs cut along its back. They are not letters and not runes. He has seen writing and is sure this is how it goes.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 4.10.4.2: an antler comb of about 960-1070 with signs that are neither letters nor runes

easter_eggs.text: In the last years of the game a boy on the row plays a pipe of grey-white fired clay, two tubes of it tied side by side. Nobody has seen another like it, then or since.
easter_eggs.source: Archeologie in West-Friesland 13: two pipes of a pan flute of Pingsdorf ware, 1050-1150, without parallel. (A thing seen, not heard: the game's music is set aside)

easter_eggs.text: In a hard frost, late in the game, the bank is littered with runners cut from horses' foot bones and pricker poles tipped with cattle bone, made in a morning. At the thaw they are thrown in the ditch.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 4.10.4: a runner of horse bone, about 1050-1135, and cattle-bone pole tips, made in haste and discarded

easter_eggs.text: Look for the mint that King Otto's charter of 985 gives away with the toll. There is none. No coin of these centuries has ever been found here; the clerk wrote toll, mint and rent because that is what clerks write.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 2.2.2.2, 2.3.3, 6.3: the charter's 'moneta'; no early medieval coin found; the first coin struck here is of 1280

easter_eggs.text: The drain ditch that runs to the stream beside Tado's ground is full of what the row has thrown away for a hundred years: bone, shoe leather, sherds, a broken glass bowl. Somebody will be very pleased with it one day.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 4.6.5.3: a drain ditch square to the river, filled 675-725 and 850-925

easter_eggs.text: There is no sea to the south, only the Almere: fresh enough to drink at the Vecht mouth. An old man says his grandfather's grandfather walked dry to Wieringen. The water is coming all the same.
easter_eggs.source: WAR 61 1.1 and 2.3.4: the Almere fresh to weakly brackish, Texel and Wieringen not yet islands, no Zuiderzee before the flood of 1170

unlocks.what: Freedom of the king's toll at Medemelacha: a cut stick from the toll man, later a sealed word from Count Ansfried.
unlocks.how: Before 813: carry Saint Martin's tenth safely to Traiectum for Radward at Martinmas, or end the night boats by telling him. From 985: bring Ansfried what Saint Martin's needs (wax, wine, oil) three times.

unlocks.what: A plot on the house row with its own length of bank.
unlocks.how: Pay for the work 'A length of the bank', or be given it by the row after the share of 810 or the flood of 838.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_plot_medemelacha; opens the jetty and the salting house; goods may be stored here

unlocks.what: The inland water by night: the channels of the Almere and the lake of Wervershoof without a light.
unlocks.how: Be a fast friend of Eilbern, by either road: as his partner at the stakes, or as the one who bought him out of it.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_pilot_almere; no grounding on the Almere in fog or dark; a day saved between the Vecht mouth and the Vlie

unlocks.what: Eilbern as a sworn partner with a second boat on the inland water.
unlocks.how: The ending 'bought_him_out' of the boats at the eel stakes.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_partner_eilbern; a second bottom carrying your goods between Dorestad, Traiectum and here

unlocks.what: A trusted household at the lake that keeps and sells your goods when you are away.
unlocks.how: Take Adelgard's tally in the flood winter and see it paid.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_factor_medemelacha; goods left here sell slowly at the row's price; first choice of the Martinmas beef and cheese

unlocks.what: Kin in Meinburg's house: a marriage or a fostering.
unlocks.how: Eight calls and no line through your mark; then say yes when she asks whether you have met her daughter.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_kin_meinburgs_house; free lodging; an heir's feelings here are not halved at the succession

unlocks.what: Word of a pot of silver in the ground on the west cliff of Wieringen.
unlocks.how: Be a fast friend of Gunnulf, and come back after 873 when he is gone and nobody else has asked.
unlocks.gives: open_fetch westerklief (hoards_793.json); a fetch across the water north-west to Wieringen

unlocks.what: Tado's kept-back querns and the first sound stones of each spring at his own price.
unlocks.how: Bring him word from across the sea of what length of black stone the English king asked for, after the peace of 796; or bring him sound roughouts from Colonia twice.
unlocks.gives: a standing commission for quernstones here at a premium; Tado a fast friend; the mossy stone, in the end, as a gift
